answer_sql: SELECT * FROM customers WHERE segment = 'Premium';

business_scenario: Find order items purchased between 1 January and 30 June 2026.
solution_approach: I will filter order items to dates between January and June 2026.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE item_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-06-30';

business_scenario: Calculate the average order value across all retail orders.
solution_approach: I will calculate the average order total across all orders.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT AVG(order_total) AS average_amount FROM orders;

business_scenario: Find the largest single line item purchase amount recorded in order items.
solution_approach: I will use MAX on amount to find the largest event value.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT MAX(amount) AS largest_amount FROM order_items;

business_scenario: Count distinct customer shipping cities represented in the order history.
solution_approach: I will count the distinct city values in customers.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT city) AS city_count FROM customers;

business_scenario: Return fulfilled orders with status Completed for monthly revenue accounting.
solution_approach: I will keep order items whose status is Completed.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE status = 'Completed';

business_scenario: Classify customer orders into High, Medium, or Low value tiers using order total.
solution_approach: I will use CASE on order total with 100000 and 50000 boundaries.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT order_id, order_total, CASE WHEN order_total >= 100000 THEN 'High' WHEN order_total >= 50000 THEN 'Medium' ELSE 'Low' END AS amount_band FROM orders ORDER BY order_id;

business_scenario: Find Active customer orders with an order total of at least 50000 requiring management dispatch sign-off.
solution_approach: I will require Active status and order total of at least 50000.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'Active' AND order_total >= 50000;

business_scenario: Show each customers name with its orders details.
solution_approach: I will join customers to orders using customer id.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT m.customer_name, r.order_id, r.status, r.order_total FROM customers m JOIN orders r ON m.customer_id=r.customer_id ORDER BY m.customer_id,r.order_id;

business_scenario: Count orders for every products item.
solution_approach: I will left join products to orders by product id. I will group each products item and count matching orders.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT c.product_name, COUNT(r.order_id) AS record_count FROM products c LEFT JOIN orders r ON c.product_id=r.product_id GROUP BY c.product_id,c.product_name ORDER BY c.product_id;

business_scenario: Find orders that have no order items.
solution_approach: I will left join order items to orders on order id and keep orders with a null order item id.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT r.order_id FROM orders r LEFT JOIN order_items e ON r.order_id=e.order_id WHERE e.order_item_id IS NULL ORDER BY r.order_id;

business_scenario: Calculate total event amount for each orders.
solution_approach: I will join orders to order items using order id. I will group by order id and sum event amounts.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT r.order_id, COALESCE(SUM(e.amount),0) AS total_amount FROM orders r LEFT JOIN order_items e ON r.order_id=e.order_id GROUP BY r.order_id ORDER BY r.order_id;

business_scenario: Find orders whose total event amount exceeds 20000.
solution_approach: I will join orders and order items and group by order id to sum event amounts. I will use HAVING to keep totals above 20000.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT r.order_id, SUM(e.amount) AS total_amount FROM orders r JOIN order_items e ON r.order_id=e.order_id GROUP BY r.order_id HAVING SUM(e.amount)>20000 ORDER BY total_amount DESC;

business_scenario: Count orders by customers segment.
solution_approach: I will link orders to customers by customer id. I will group by segment and count the matching orders.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT m.segment, COUNT(r.order_id) AS record_count FROM customers m LEFT JOIN orders r ON m.customer_id=r.customer_id GROUP BY m.segment ORDER BY m.segment;

business_scenario: Calculate average order_total by products category.
solution_approach: I will join products and orders by product id. I will group by category and average order total.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT c.category, AVG(r.order_total) AS average_amount FROM products c JOIN orders r ON c.product_id=r.product_id GROUP BY c.category ORDER BY c.category;

business_scenario: Show customers, orders and products names together.
solution_approach: I will join customers, orders and products through customer id and product id to show customer name, product name, and status.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT m.customer_name, r.order_id, c.product_name, r.status FROM customers m JOIN orders r ON m.customer_id=r.customer_id JOIN products c ON r.product_id=c.product_id ORDER BY r.order_id;

business_scenario: Calculate total order_total for each customers.
solution_approach: I will join customers and orders and sum order total for each customers.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT m.customer_id,m.customer_name,SUM(r.order_total) AS total_amount FROM customers m JOIN orders r ON m.customer_id=r.customer_id GROUP BY m.customer_id,m.customer_name ORDER BY total_amount DESC;

business_scenario: Find orders whose order_total is above the overall average.
solution_approach: I will compare each order total in orders with the overall average from a subquery.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT order_id,order_total FROM orders WHERE order_total>(SELECT AVG(order_total) FROM orders) ORDER BY order_total DESC;

business_scenario: Show order items with their parent orders status.
solution_approach: I will join order items to orders using the parent key.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT e.order_item_id,e.item_date,e.item_type,e.amount,r.status AS record_status FROM order_items e JOIN orders r ON e.order_id=r.order_id ORDER BY e.order_item_id;

business_scenario: Calculate completed and failed event amounts for every orders.
solution_approach: I will join orders and order items and use CASE inside SUM for Completed and Failed event amounts.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT r.order_id,SUM(CASE WHEN e.status='Completed' THEN e.amount ELSE 0 END) AS completed_amount,SUM(CASE WHEN e.status='Failed' THEN e.amount ELSE 0 END) AS failed_amount FROM orders r LEFT JOIN order_items e ON r.order_id=e.order_id GROUP BY r.order_id ORDER BY r.order_id;

business_scenario: Count order items by calendar month.
solution_approach: I will derive the month from item date, group order items and count each month.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month',item_date)::date AS event_month,COUNT(*) AS event_count FROM order_items GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month',item_date) ORDER BY event_month;

business_scenario: Find customers with no orders.
solution_approach: I will left join orders to customers on customer id and keep customers with no orders key.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT m.customer_id,m.customer_name FROM customers m LEFT JOIN orders r ON m.customer_id=r.customer_id WHERE r.order_id IS NULL ORDER BY m.customer_id;

business_scenario: Find products items that are unused by orders.
solution_approach: I will left join orders to products on product id and keep products with no matching orders.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT c.product_id,c.product_name FROM products c LEFT JOIN orders r ON c.product_id=r.product_id WHERE r.order_id IS NULL ORDER BY c.product_id;

business_scenario: Find the earliest orders date for every customers.
solution_approach: I will join customers and orders, group by customer id and take the minimum order date.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT m.customer_id,m.customer_name,MIN(r.order_date) AS first_date FROM customers m JOIN orders r ON m.customer_id=r.customer_id GROUP BY m.customer_id,m.customer_name ORDER BY m.customer_id;

business_scenario: Find the latest order items date for every orders.
solution_approach: I will left join order items to orders, group by order id and take the maximum item date.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT r.order_id,MAX(e.item_date) AS latest_event_date FROM orders r LEFT JOIN order_items e ON r.order_id=e.order_id GROUP BY r.order_id ORDER BY r.order_id;

business_scenario: List distinct customers with at least one completed order items.
solution_approach: I will join customers, orders and order items, keep Completed events and remove duplicate customers.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT DISTINCT m.customer_id,m.customer_name FROM customers m JOIN orders r ON m.customer_id=r.customer_id JOIN order_items e ON r.order_id=e.order_id WHERE e.status='Completed' ORDER BY m.customer_id;

business_scenario: Calculate average event amount by products category.
solution_approach: I will join products, orders and order items through their keys. I will group by category and average event amount.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT c.category,AVG(e.amount) AS average_event_amount FROM products c JOIN orders r ON c.product_id=r.product_id JOIN order_items e ON r.order_id=e.order_id GROUP BY c.category ORDER BY c.category;

business_scenario: Count orders by master segment and record status.
solution_approach: I will join customers and orders and group counts by segment and status.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT m.segment,r.status,COUNT(*) AS record_count FROM customers m JOIN orders r ON m.customer_id=r.customer_id GROUP BY m.segment,r.status ORDER BY m.segment,r.status;

business_scenario: Rank customers by total event amount.
solution_approach: I will join customers, orders and order items and total event amounts per customers. I will rank the totals from highest to lowest.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: WITH totals AS (SELECT m.customer_id,m.customer_name,SUM(e.amount) total_amount FROM customers m JOIN orders r ON m.customer_id=r.customer_id JOIN order_items e ON r.order_id=e.order_id GROUP BY m.customer_id,m.customer_name) SELECT customer_id,customer_name,total_amount,RANK() OVER(ORDER BY total_amount DESC) AS amount_rank FROM totals ORDER BY amount_rank,customer_id;

business_scenario: Find orders whose latest event was before 1 January 2026 or is missing.
solution_approach: I will left join order items to orders using order id so orders without activity remain. I will group each orders by order id and use HAVING on its latest item date.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT r.order_id,MAX(e.item_date) AS latest_event_date FROM orders r LEFT JOIN order_items e ON r.order_id=e.order_id GROUP BY r.order_id HAVING MAX(e.item_date)<DATE '2026-01-01' OR MAX(e.item_date) IS NULL ORDER BY r.order_id;

business_scenario: Find customers whose total order_total is above the average master total.
solution_approach: I will use a CTE to total order total by customer id in orders. I will keep customers totals above the average total.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: WITH totals AS (SELECT customer_id,SUM(order_total) total_amount FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) SELECT customer_id,total_amount FROM totals WHERE total_amount>(SELECT AVG(total_amount) FROM totals) ORDER BY total_amount DESC;

business_scenario: Classify orders into High, Medium and Low amount bands.
solution_approach: I will classify orders using CASE with 100000 and 50000 order total boundaries.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT order_id,order_total,CASE WHEN order_total>=100000 THEN 'High' WHEN order_total>=50000 THEN 'Medium' ELSE 'Low' END amount_band FROM orders ORDER BY order_id;

business_scenario: Show month-over-month event amount for every orders.
solution_approach: I will total event amounts in order items by order id and month in a CTE. I will use LAG partitioned by order id and ordered by event month.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: WITH monthly AS (SELECT order_id,DATE_TRUNC('month',item_date)::date event_month,SUM(amount) monthly_amount FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id,DATE_TRUNC('month',item_date)) SELECT order_id,event_month,monthly_amount,LAG(monthly_amount) OVER(PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY event_month) previous_month_amount FROM monthly ORDER BY order_id,event_month;

business_scenario: Calculate a running event total within every orders.
solution_approach: I will use a windowed SUM of amount in order items partitioned by order id and ordered by item date and order item id.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT order_id,order_item_id,item_date,amount,SUM(amount) OVER(PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY item_date,order_item_id) running_amount FROM order_items ORDER BY order_id,item_date,order_item_id;

business_scenario: Return the two largest order items for every order id.
solution_approach: I will assign row numbers within each order id in order items by descending amount. I will keep row numbers 1 and 2 for every order id.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: WITH ranked AS (SELECT e.*,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY amount DESC,order_item_id) rn FROM order_items e) SELECT order_item_id,order_id,amount FROM ranked WHERE rn<=2 ORDER BY order_id,rn;

business_scenario: Calculate each orders share of total event amount.
solution_approach: I will join orders and order items to total amounts for each orders in a CTE. I will divide each orders total by the windowed grand total.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: WITH totals AS (SELECT r.order_id,COALESCE(SUM(e.amount),0) total_amount FROM orders r LEFT JOIN order_items e ON r.order_id=e.order_id GROUP BY r.order_id) SELECT order_id,total_amount,ROUND(100.0*total_amount/NULLIF(SUM(total_amount) OVER(),0),2) percent_of_total FROM totals ORDER BY order_id;

business_scenario: Dense-rank orders by order_total within each customers.
solution_approach: I will dense rank orders within each customer id by descending order total.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT customer_id,order_id,order_total,DENSE_RANK() OVER(PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_total DESC) amount_rank FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id,amount_rank,order_id;

business_scenario: Show each event amount beside the previous event amount.
solution_approach: I will use LAG in order items partitioned by order id ordered by item date and order item id.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT order_id,order_item_id,item_date,amount,LAG(amount) OVER(PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY item_date,order_item_id) previous_amount FROM order_items ORDER BY order_id,item_date,order_item_id;

business_scenario: Calculate a three-event moving average for each orders.
solution_approach: I will average the current and two preceding amounts in order items partitioned by order id ordered by item date and order item id.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT order_id,order_item_id,item_date,amount,AVG(amount) OVER(PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY item_date,order_item_id ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) moving_average FROM order_items ORDER BY order_id,item_date,order_item_id;

business_scenario: Find customers whose every orders is Active.
solution_approach: I will use EXISTS to require that each customers has at least one orders. I will use NOT EXISTS to exclude customers with a non-Active orders.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT m.customer_id,m.customer_name FROM customers m WHERE EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM orders r WHERE r.customer_id=m.customer_id) AND NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM orders r WHERE r.customer_id=m.customer_id AND r.status<>'Active') ORDER BY m.customer_id;

business_scenario: Find orders above the average order_total for their status.
solution_approach: I will compare each orders with the average order total for its own status.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT order_id,status,order_total FROM orders r WHERE order_total>(SELECT AVG(x.order_total) FROM orders x WHERE x.status=r.status) ORDER BY status,order_total DESC;

business_scenario: Calculate days between the first and last event for each orders.
solution_approach: I will join orders and order items, group by order id and take minimum and maximum item date. I will subtract the first date from the last date to get active days.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT r.order_id,MIN(e.item_date) first_event,MAX(e.item_date) last_event,MAX(e.item_date)-MIN(e.item_date) active_days FROM orders r JOIN order_items e ON r.order_id=e.order_id GROUP BY r.order_id ORDER BY r.order_id;

business_scenario: Calculate every event's percentage contribution to its orders total.
solution_approach: I will divide each order items amount by the total amount within its order id partition.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT order_item_id,order_id,amount,ROUND(100.0*amount/NULLIF(SUM(amount) OVER(PARTITION BY order_id),0),2) record_percent FROM order_items ORDER BY order_id,order_item_id;

business_scenario: Return the highest-value customers in each segment.
solution_approach: I will join customers and orders to total order total for every customers and segment. I will row-number within each segment and keep rank 1.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: WITH totals AS (SELECT m.customer_id,m.customer_name,m.segment,SUM(r.order_total) total_amount FROM customers m JOIN orders r ON m.customer_id=r.customer_id GROUP BY m.customer_id,m.customer_name,m.segment), ranked AS (SELECT *,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY segment ORDER BY total_amount DESC,customer_id) rn FROM totals) SELECT customer_id,customer_name,segment,total_amount FROM ranked WHERE rn=1 ORDER BY segment;

business_scenario: Find order items whose amount is above their parent record average.
solution_approach: I will compare each order items amount with the average amount for its parent order id.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT order_item_id,order_id,amount FROM order_items e WHERE amount>(SELECT AVG(x.amount) FROM order_items x WHERE x.order_id=e.order_id) ORDER BY order_id,amount DESC;

business_scenario: Find customers whose record count is above the average master record count.
solution_approach: I will left join customers and orders and count orders for every customers in a CTE. I will keep customers counts above the average master count.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: WITH counts AS (SELECT m.customer_id,m.customer_name,COUNT(r.order_id) record_count FROM customers m LEFT JOIN orders r ON m.customer_id=r.customer_id GROUP BY m.customer_id,m.customer_name) SELECT customer_id,customer_name,record_count FROM counts WHERE record_count>(SELECT AVG(record_count) FROM counts) ORDER BY record_count DESC,customer_id;

business_scenario: Show completed, pending and failed event totals per orders.
solution_approach: I will join orders and order items to conditionally sum Completed, Pending and Failed event amounts per orders.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT r.order_id,SUM(CASE WHEN e.status='Completed' THEN e.amount ELSE 0 END) completed_amount,SUM(CASE WHEN e.status='Pending' THEN e.amount ELSE 0 END) pending_amount,SUM(CASE WHEN e.status='Failed' THEN e.amount ELSE 0 END) failed_amount FROM orders r LEFT JOIN order_items e ON r.order_id=e.order_id GROUP BY r.order_id ORDER BY r.order_id;

business_scenario: Return the latest order items row for every order id.
solution_approach: I will row number order items partitioned by order id from newest to oldest by item date and order item id. I will keep row number 1 as the latest event.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: WITH ranked AS (SELECT e.*,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY item_date DESC,order_item_id DESC) rn FROM order_items e) SELECT order_item_id,order_id,item_date,item_type,amount,status FROM ranked WHERE rn=1 ORDER BY order_id;
